title: Kyrin the Lost
type: Freed captive · witness to lost Babel
dek: A survivor of petrification whose fragmented memories preserve a beautiful land and the pain of its loss.

facts.Condition: Freed from petrification; damaged and incomplete memory
facts.Past: Remembers forts, farms, vineyards and the Tree’s waters on Ashur
facts.Last witnessed: Skylight Refuge · 5, Month of Moirah, Year 3
facts.Priority: Safety for the children; no confirmed complete restoration

sources: Babel quest record · campfire testimony, August 2026
body:
Kyrin the Lost is a freed captive whose memories preserve a beautiful Babel before its ruin. At Skylight Refuge, he speaks plainly about what was taken from him and insists that questions about his mind be put to him directly. His grief does not make him a silent object of rescue.

The right to answer for himself

Arjahn begins by asking another survivor what imprisonment in stone might have done to a man the company freed. He admits that they could not move the other prisoners and that he destroyed many statues in an attempt to end their suffering. Kyrin interrupts the discussion of his mind by pointing out that the question can be addressed to him.

Arjahn recognizes the mistake and apologizes. Kyrin calls himself the Lost, in battle, memory and soul, and initially accepts that he deserved to be dismissed. Arjahn rejects that judgment. Their exchange begins with a correction in who gets to speak, before it can become a useful source of information.

The land he remembers

Kyrin remembers mountain forts, valley farms and vineyards, followed by the sky falling and the tree breaking. He names the floating island Ashur and recalls abundant waters from its tree. The memory belongs to a distressed witness; neither its ancient date nor every cause of the catastrophe is settled by his recollection.

The waters of Ashur

Kyrin’s surviving picture of the old land is specific: mountain forts, valley farms and vineyards. He remembers the sky dropping on the valley, the Tree shattering and crushing the land. When Arjahn asks where the Tree stood, Kyrin places it on the floating island of Ashur.

He remembers abundance and pure water flowing from above. Asked about magical protection that prevents the adventurers from reaching the island, he answers from a different past: to him, it had simply been beautiful. That contrast tells the company what has been lost without explaining exactly when every barrier or occupation began. The earlier ridge expedition supplies the separate observation of its frozen city and the caldera below.

Help without speaking over him

Arjahn initially asks someone else about the freed man’s mind, then apologizes for not addressing him directly. He explains that bodily healing is not the same as repairing memory or a soul, and offers support without promising an instant cure. Kyrin blames his own people’s failure to defend their land; Arjahn rejects that blame and insists that being attacked was not their fault.

Kyrin asks that the children be sent away from danger. He refuses to romanticize his captor and says surviving captives might know more than he does. Those possibilities remain leads, not completed rescues or recovered memories.

Grief, blame and the children

The memory of the ruined land makes Kyrin ask that the children be sent away. He apologizes as though his people had ruined it themselves. Arjahn becomes firm: being attacked was not their fault, and surviving under such pressure is no small thing. He promises to keep fighting while trying to speak gently enough that reassurance does not become another threat.

Kyrin still names a loss of hope, courage and heritage. Arjahn offers the possibility of living on as a changed person and admits that repairing a mind or soul is different from healing a body. Neither the comfort nor Kyrin’s ability to converse establishes that his memories have been made whole.

What he will and will not offer about his captor

Asked whether Abyss might be made to return his memories, Kyrin doubts that the captor can be forced to do anything. When Arjahn considers exploiting the enemy’s single-mindedness, Kyrin sharply refuses language that could soften what the captor has done. Arjahn clarifies that he means a tactical weakness, not forgiveness.

Kyrin does not claim to be a general or to understand every purpose behind his imprisonment. He says other remaining captives might know more and offers to point the adventurers toward those possibilities. The offer is valuable precisely because it has limits. It is a lead from a person who has survived captivity, not a recovered prisoner list or a completed second rescue.
